utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 27th of January, 2010. Let me first greet Mr. Dabic, our witness; Ms. Biersay, Mr. Marcussen, and the entire OTP team; good afternoon to you, Mr. Seselj, not to forgot of course the interpreters and all the people assisting us in our work. Sorry for the slight delay. It's just that the previous hearing finished a little late, which is why we are starting with a few minutes' delay. Ms. Biersay, based on our calculation you still have 40 minutes left. In other words, we'll try to stay within the time-limits. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dabic. I wanted to follow-up on some questions that were put to you yesterday by the Bench. Specifically, I'd like to turn your attention to the summer of 1991, around the time when you joined the SDS. You joined the SDS after going to an SDS-sponsored - now, what word would you use? - gathering or rally?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, I was at this gathering, and I joined the Serbian Democratic Party. It was the only party that was predominant in the Neretva River Valley and which rallied the Serb people, whereas the Muslim people had their SDA, the Party of Democratic Action; and the Croatian people had the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, that rally, from what I understand, started in Mostar and then went to Nevesinje -- sorry, the gathering, it started in Mostar and then it went to Nevesinje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood it well. The meeting at Mostar was at the football-pitch of the football club Velez. There were about 3.000 people and the weather was very stormy, whereas the meeting in Nevesinje took place somewhat later. I don't remember the date, but I was present at that meeting too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Approximately how many people attended the gathering in the Nevesinje town square in that period in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Nevesinje perhaps 500 people more, so 3.500, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could ask the Registry for what has been marked as MFI 880, and specifically I'd like to go to the -- in the English it's page 8, the B/C/S will be page 6, and it begins with -- the paragraph begins with: "The main speakers present were ..." to find the B/C/S. The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the paragraph with the number 15- to 20.000 Serbs which is a paragraph up from the bar. I'm showing you this because in your 2000 statement to the OTP you said that there were approximately -- you estimated that there were approximately 15- to 20.000 Serbs at that rally. Does that refresh your recollection about which --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the rally was in front of the sports hall, and in front of that sports hall there were about three and a half thousand men, maybe 4.000. But the others were probably walking around town and the surroundings, but in my estimate there were about 3.500 people in front of the city hall because the square there is not really big.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So where were the other 15 -- the other people that you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were probably in Nevesinje in the various coffee bars in Nevesinje and the surroundings, because I stayed there for about an hour, an hour and a half, and then I left. And we were expecting -- I'm sorry, we were expecting Radovan Karadzic to arrive, Krajisnik, and Koljevic, but I left with my colleague. And then maybe later on the number increased to 10- or 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you why you said that there were 15- to 20.000 Serbs at this rally in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned with my friend to Mostar, we learnt that the number of people did go up to 15- to 20.000. In the immediate vicinity of the sports hall there was the football stadium, and the stadium can take 10- to 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: From the national SDS party, which officials attended the rally that you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Krajisnik, Koljevic, and the president at the time of the municipality of Nevesinje, Vukan Bratic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know someone by the name of Krsto Savic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krsto Savic, I do know him very well. I know that he's from Nevesinje and he's married, or rather, his wife --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me be more precise. Do -- you are familiar with someone named Krsto Savic. Are you saying that you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any personal contact with him, but I do know him. I know he worked in the police and I would see him, and I was going to say that I know his wife very well because she's from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What position did he hold during the time-period of -- in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 he was chief of the civilian police in Nevesinje, and before that he held that post too, head of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did he -- was he present at this rally that you just described to the members of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, normally he was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why do you say "normally"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he is chief of the police station, the police had to attend to secure the rallies, so as to prevent any incident from occurring. Because in those days, apart from the Orthodox people in Nevesinje - to put it that way - there were people of other ethnicities too. There were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Arsen Grahovac, could you tell us whether or not he attended the rally you just described?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did. I don't remember, but I think he did because it was very crowded and I wasn't close to the stage to see everyone there. But on the loud-speaker system they announced the arrival of guests.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you hear his arrival being announced?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear it because he's a local. He's from Nevesinje. In those days he wasn't that important. So Radovan Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Koljevic were far more significant at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In very brief terms, what was the general message about the situation that Serbs faced?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember, but I think -- no, I don't think. I'm a hundred percentage sure that at this gathering or rally - as you call it - there was no call for a conflict against the non-Serb population in eastern Herzegovina, that would be against the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did they say about the situation that Serbs faced?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I think -- as I was saying, they weren't inciting any kind of conflict or war or saying that these people should be expelled --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand, I understand. You're saying that you don't remember what they said about the situation that Serbs faced at this rally?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- thank you. At this rally were there officials from surrounding villages or towns as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, mostly people from the surrounding villages came, such as Bileca, Gacko, or Trebinje. There -- the presidents of those municipalities. These are not villages, these are towns, so they were there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "presidents" of these towns, what do you mean presidents, presidents of what?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our country we usually call them town mayors. For instance, the town mayor of Nevesinje, the town mayor of Trebinje or the president -- it's easier to say the president of the municipality because Trebinje is a municipality; it's not a big town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The surrounding villages that you just mentioned, were they predominantly Serb were they predominantly something else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large extent they were Serb, but the places I mentioned were inhabited predominantly by Serb Orthodox inhabitants, but there were also Muslims living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to move from 1991, and now I'd like to direct your attention to the time-frame of May to June of 1992. You describe for the Trial Chamber that at some point in May of 1992 that you joined the Mostar TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For what part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the eastern part of Mostar where I lived, the eastern part of the town, because the town of Mostar is divided by the Neretva River. So you have the eastern and the western part, so I was in the eastern part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did that TO have a predominant ethnicity, the people in that TO, what were they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I can remember, to the best of my recollection, there were some Muslims and some Croat inhabitants too, not in large numbers. The predominant ethnicity was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With respect to Mostar, could you tell us where Podvelezje is in relation to Mostar and Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podvelezje in relation to Mostar and Nevesinje is below Mount Velez, which dominates the town of Mostar. It is some 20 kilometres away; however, Mount Velez cannot be seen from the eastern part of the town. So it is more or less on the road between Mostar and Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement - and I won't go through it - you describe many factors that were in Mostar. Was there an aluminium factory in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar in the western part of the town -- or rather, in the southern part of the town in the direction of the coast there was a large aluminium factory that was operating rather well and it co-operated with the aluminium factory in Sibenik, Split, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did that factory make military products?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aluminium factory in Mostar did not manufacture military products. It was simply aluminium that they were manufacturing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the name of that factory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the Aluminium Kombinat or combined factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you heard of a factory by the name of Sokol, S-o-k-o-l?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to express it. Even small children knew of this factory. Of course I'd heard of the Sokol factory --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is it --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And while I was -- very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What kind of factory is it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sokol factory in Mostar was a military factory manufacturing and making parts for military planes, and it manufactured aircraft and helicopters, planes, and helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you have described in your statement and to the questions posed by the Trial Chamber what Seselj's men meant to you, and I don't want to go through that again. What I do want to ask you is that: Are you aware that a man by the name of Branislav Vakic was made a Vojvoda in part because of his contributions in Serbian Herzegovina in May and June 1992? Did you know that? Did you know of that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hear of that man for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know that Branislav Vakic has talked about being in Nevesinje with the forces there? Are you aware of that? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam -- no. How can I be aware of that when I don't know the man?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, I understand. I have to --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have to get you to say yes or no before I can ask the next question. Because you say no, then I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness didn't say "no." He said he doesn't know. It's one thing when he says he doesn't know, and it's another matter if he says no. The witness didn't say that Vakic wasn't there because we have been saying for some time that Vakic was there, but the witness said that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now on record. Please continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How much time do I have available, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. Can the Registrar tell us. I think you must have taken 20 minutes already, so I guess you have about 20 minutes left -- actually 15 so says the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how -- just to be clear, for how long were you active in the Mostar TO from May to June, just so we have that perfectly clear in the record?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make it quite clear for you, I was there from May until the 13th of June, when I was wounded and transported to the hospital in Titograd, now called Podgorica, and then on to the rehabilitation centre in Meljine near Herceg Novi, where I spent two months for rehabilitation. I'm really sorry I don't have the document to prove to you that this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me return to something that was said earlier on because it may turn out to be extremely important. Regarding Branislav Vakic, did you know him or did you not know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, believe me, it is the first time in this Tribunal for me to hear of that man. It really is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is why I was asking you that question. We have a document that has been admitted, Exhibit 1841 - I don't have the exact number - but we have all the Vojvodas that were appointed by Mr. Seselj because we can see his name here and this one is under number 3. And I have also his record. It was said that he was a unit commander, a Chetnik Serbian unit commander in Serbian Herzegovina in May and June 1992, so May and June 1992. So this is the question put by Madam Prosecutor. He took part in the battles of Klepci, Tasovcici, and Mostar. He also commanded units of the Chetnik Serbian Movement in Skelani and took part in final operation in Brcko, Zitnic, and Drnis. Now, I'm interested in this period from May to June 1992. We have Klepci, this is close to Mostar, Tasovcici. Did you know that there were -- that there was fighting there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, during those two months that I spent in Mostar, I went to Nevesinje only once and that is the moment I was wounded. But you are right, there were battles in Tasovcici and Klepci. But regarding this individual that you say Dr. Vojislav Seselj appointed a Vojvoda, I hear of him for the first time, truly. Please believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There was ongoing fighting over there, but who commanded the troops? Was it the TO? The VRS? JNA? According to you, who commanded all these troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the commander of the defence in the Neretva River Valley, that is to say from Salakovac -- well, Salakovac is about 17 kilometres away from Mostar on the road towards Sarajevo, and then from Salakovac to Tasovcici, it was the late Branko Simic from Zitomislic, which is a very small locality. So he was the main commander for the entire Neretva river valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. According to you the name of the commander was Branko Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100 per cent sure. And he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- death, he died a natural death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know who this commander reported to. Did he report to the municipality under -- for TO reasons? Did he report to the JNA? To the commander of the VRS, the notorious General Mladic? Who did this person report to? Mr. Seselj? Mr. Karadzic? Who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was subordinated to the Serb Democratic Party because he was in the Presidency of the Serb Democratic Party too. So it is the party that appointed him commander, or rather, made him in charge of the defence of the Neretva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. This is important. You are saying that he was subordinated to the Serb Democratic Party. Who was the president of this party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think -- well, excuse me for my language, but I think that even the birds and trees know, everyone knows that it was Dr. Radovan Karadzic. At the time he was president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you correctly, you say that everyone knows it. Very well. But it has to be on record. If I understand you correctly, we have Radovan Karadzic, president of the Serbian Radical Party --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Democratic Party, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- appointing as person to be in charge of the TO this person called Branko Simic, heading the TO; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's clearly noted on the record, and if I understood correctly there is fighting, there is ongoing fighting, there are units, and maybe among these units we could find this famous Branislav Vakic but we don't know that, but that's the way the structure is organised. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on your questions, I'd advise the Trial Chamber that 65 ter number 1910 in your binders also pertains to Branislav Vakic. It specifically is a -- I believe it is an October 12th, 1993, transcript from the Serbian Assembly session, and it was republished in Mr. Seselj's book "The Hard Fall of the Government," and in that exhibit at page 4 going to page 5, it describes what Mr. Vakic says about his participation in Nevesinje and in the Podvelezje area. Now, as this witness says he doesn't know him, I won't be putting it to him. But should the Trial Chamber find it helpful, I would tender that into evidence to assist the Court. And in conjunction with that, there is another exhibit which currently does have an MNA status, and that is the accompanying certificate that he talks about with respect to Podvelezje, and that is MNA P649 and it should be a supplement to your binder as 65 ter number 1636, to assist the Court. And also to assist the Court, the order that you just described to the witness is in evidence as Exhibit P217.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This is an absolutely impermissible method of conducting a cross-examination and tendering documents into evidence. Goran Stoparic was the first prosecution witness that they called, and he testified that he was in Vakic's unit. He testified that as a member of Vakic's unit he came to Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to Mr. Seselj testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he took part in the fighting --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If he has an objection, he --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't let her interrupt me. You see how she is shouting at me, Ms. Biersay. That is impermissible. You would have thrown me out of the courtroom if I was speaking that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, up until now everything ran very smoothly and you behaved yourself extremely well up until now. The cross -- you will soon be cross-examining this witness because Ms. Biersay is almost done with her own cross. You will be able to check things with this witness, even if there are things he doesn't know. There are things he know, and you can mention all this during your cross-examination. So please let Ms. Biersay finish her own cross-examination, and then you'll have plenty of time --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Ms. Biersay tendered some documents into evidence and I am objecting to that proposal of her's, and it is my right to object as soon as a proposal is being made. If you are denying me that right and if you are calling my current behaviour indecent, then you can throw me out of the courtroom and I won't mind. As soon as you tell me that you're throwing me out I'm going to get up and walk out, but I am right on this: As soon as Ms. Biersay makes a proposal, I have the right to object to that proposal. I am explaining why it is that I object to her proposal, and Ms. Biersay did not do that in a timely fashion. This is a witness who had never heard of Branislav Vakic, and then tendering documents related to Vakic ten pages long in relation to this witness, whereas you had here as a Prosecution witness a man whose commander Branislav Vakic was, and that was the opportunity to tender these documents. That is why I say it's impermissible. As a matter of fact, it is in my interest to have that admitted into evidence, but for matters -- as a matter of principle, I am opposing the admission of that document into evidence. And now you can throw me out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, no one wants to chase you out of this courtroom; absolutely not. We're doing our utmost to make sure that you stay in the courtroom. And you're right, Ms. Biersay was tendering a document and you can raise objections, which is what you did, fine. But I thought your objection had to do with the substance of the matter and not with the admission of the document, especially since one of the documents among these mentioned has already been admitted anyway. Ms. Biersay, if I understood you correctly, all the documents you mentioned were documents that you were tendering. I hadn't noted that, but now I found that out, and Mr. Seselj raised an objection. Is this what you really asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not eliminating that as a possibility, but my offer to the Court was to bring it to the Court's attention because of the Court's questions. And the Court correctly seized on the value and role of Mr. Vakic, and I am advising the Court that 65 ter number 1910 and 1636 are pertinent to the Court's questions. Should the Court deem it appropriate, we would - and certainly the Court can also - move it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are not tendering this document as of now. Very well, please pursue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to in the time we have left move to the video that we saw yesterday, and the entire video as I understand it has been admitted as P -- sorry, MFI P879, and we played two clips yesterday that I would ask the Court to be assigned either -- to be assigned numbers apart from the 40-minute one that has this number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, yesterday we saw two videos, two clips, one which was an interview of Grahovac and the other one had to do with interviews between a journalist and a number of soldiers at night. So we need two numbers, two MFI numbers first of course, because the Trial Chamber will rule on this later on after the cross-examination. So could we please have two numbers for these two clips.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first clip will be P886 marked for identification, and the second one will be P887, MFI as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dabic, could I confirm with you what I believe you said yesterday was that the Ravna Gora -- is it a restaurant or a tavern in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a sort of tavern --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- cafe. The word we use is "gostiona" and over here they say "kafic."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did that serve as a base for the Karadjordje unit?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it. I doubt it that it was a base.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now if I could please have the clip A that we played yesterday, and if we could go to one hour -- the time code one hour, 15 minutes, and 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, again this is MFI P886. Could you -- are you able to see the caption before you? Can you read the -- what it says?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. Of course I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you loud and clear what is written here in Cyrillic letters is: Arsen Grahovac, commander of the Serb Volunteer Detachment. However, the word "Karadjordje" is missing and it was written yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours, objection Judges, this question is wrong. The Prosecutor is supposed to ask whether the witness recognises the man on the monitor, not ask whether he can read this out. Let's hear the witness whether he can recognise this man as being Arsen Grahovac or not. That is the only relevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this supposed to prove, that the witness knows all the letters of the alphabet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, witness, I thought I understood that you had seen him once, this Arsen Grahovac, so that it was so obvious that it went without saying. But since we have an objection, could you please tell us whether you had seen Arsen Grahovac and whether you recognise him here on -- whether it's him that we see on screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this picture here in front of me on the monitor, on my right-hand side there is the Yutel journalist of this Yugoslav television. I don't know his name. And on the left-hand side is the late Arsen Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay asked you to read the caption out loud. Could you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arsen Grahovac, commander of the Serb Volunteer Detachment; however, I repeat yet again that word missing is "Karadjordje" and last night it was written there as far as I can remember. And I think that I do remember that well. It was actually written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, it's -- would seem that yesterday the word "Karadjordje" was on the caption, and between yesterday and this afternoon this word disappeared. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you have the footage --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- I'm addressing the Court's question, we can play just a few seconds after and perhaps that will address the witness. But for now on the record is the witness reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we're addressing that technical issue, let me ask you this. You just read this -- translated this as being the Serb Volunteer Detachment. Was that associated with some other group as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't. I don't think so. I don't think that there was some other group. As for this footage that you showed last night and right this moment, that is what I watched on television too. I remember that very well as if it were right now. However, I think that the other part of the footage was a bit dark -- well, it was at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For technical reasons we may have to play the one-minute-and-30-second clip in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dabic, does that refresh your recollection about whether you saw on the screen something that said "Karadjordje"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did see it last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, I listened to the translation in French very carefully. We have excellent interpreters translating from B/C/S into French. While listening to the late Arsen Grahovac, I can tell you that he never said that it was a group of volunteers. He said the following: These are armed civilians. It is an armed group. He said the Serbs armed themselves. I never heard in the translation I received from the B/C/S-French booth that he was a commander of a group of Serb volunteers. Therefore, the caption as it is does not seem to correspond to what is actually said in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that is a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you know Grahovac to be involved with this Serbian volunteer detachment that was listed under his name? Is that correct what they wrote under his name?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Judge put it very well, and of course I understood everything he said. There is interpretation. What was written there, Arsen Grahovac, the commander of the Serb Volunteer Detachment, that can just be rigged by that TV, Yutel --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that was to a large extent --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you -- did they say that he was a member of a Chetnik Movement that you could hear?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, and my hearing really is very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could -- if we could now move to clip B.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now playing one hour, 19 minutes, and 19 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. I am not receiving translation in French. I can see that there is an English translation, but I'd like to have directly B/C/S into French. The interpreter forgot to turn on the mike. So let's start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did the Court receive that interpretation in French?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard the following sentence, which is extremely important. One of the participants on the screen says: We only recognise Martic and Seselj and no one else. This is what I heard. We only recognise, which doesn't mean that we are members of Martic's men or Seselj's men, but we only recognise. And this is a translation we received directly from B/C/S into French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness. Witness, you don't know whether Arsen Grahovac commanded this group, yes or no, you don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, what group, Karadjordje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This group of armed civilians who suddenly went to war. As far as I'm concerned, I believe that these were volunteers. I would like to know whether you said that you did not know that he commanded this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that properly, that the late Arsen Grahovac had nothing to do with the Chetniks or some Chetnik detachment of volunteers. He was commander of the Karadjordje Detachment. However, this footage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's set the video aside for a minute. I would like to know the following. What exactly is this group which you called "Karadjordje"? Could you qualify this group? Could you tell us who made it up, who were part -- which kind of -- what kind of people were in this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were mostly people from the territory of Nevesinje municipality and the surrounding villages who organised themselves, who were huntsmen and had hunting weapons. And as this -- one of these boys said, they had some leftover from their grandfathers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I understand personally, myself, those are volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, so you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us be very specific because this may have huge repercussions. My colleague said as I understood they were volunteers, but in your view were they volunteers hailing from Serbia or local volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been proven that they were locals because this was before the outbreak of the conflict, quite a bit before it, when village guards were organised. 100 per cent this has nothing to do with volunteers from Serbia or anywhere else, nothing at all to do with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was happening almost a year before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your view, when Judge Lattanzi said "volunteers," you agreed with her but you specified that they were local volunteers, people from the area, civilians who joined that group and they hailed from that area. They were not from Belgrade or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Far from Belgrade and Serbia, far from it. These were people from the local area, the surroundings of Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no problem with that. I just wanted to know whether they were volunteers or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from Nevesinje municipality. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All the Judges agree. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the interpreter did not interpret what Judge Lattanzi just said, and you have it in the transcript in English. Let me just say that I'm constantly dissatisfied with the interpreter, especially the one who's doing it now, because he said "Klepce" instead of "Klepci." He couldn't pronounce Drnis, though I see that he is a Croat so he should know the names of Drnis and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Judge Lattanzi spoke twice. Which part are you now referring to that was allegedly not properly translated. The second time she spoke is on page 22, lines 23 and 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be specific when I said what I said. I spoke and it may be that the interpreter into English misheard or it may be that the interpreter into French did not hear me properly because my microphone was not on. I was actually speaking to the Judge, so no problem with me if this is now in the transcript. But this is not the interpreter's fault. It's my fault because I did not turn my mike on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was not interpreted for me "I have no problem with this, I just wanted to know whether they were volunteers or not." This is in the transcript and this was not interpreted for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the problem arises from the first time Judge Lattanzi spoke when she spoke about volunteers and it may be that it was not properly interpreted then. But I think that we now -- we all are in the clear. That's at least what I hope. Please, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that I have about five minutes left, and with the Court's leave what I would respectfully request is that I reserve it. There are certain issues that the Bench covered that I don't believe is necessary to cover again with the witness, but depending on the nature of Mr. Seselj's cross-examination I would ask for some latitude in using that five minutes as a kind of -- I'm not sure what to call it, but perhaps re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, but, Ms. Biersay, you were trained in the common-law system. You know better than I do that as a rule when a witness is called by the Trial Chamber and becomes a Chamber witness, nobody can ask a question after the Trial Chamber. That's one possibility. The Chamber may decide to reduce the duration of the time reserved for questions. We said that you had one hour and a half. Mr. Seselj had the same time. You now would like to keep those five minutes just in case. I'm going to ask my colleagues. I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we say that as a rule you're not allowed to have any time after the cross-examination, but since you have five minutes left you may use it if you want to use it later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Excuse me, thank you. My mike wasn't on. And I could make submissions on it later, but in the interests of time I simply want to say that we will move for the admission of the witness's 2000 statement as well as his 2004 statement that was -- that were made to the Office of the Prosecutor, specifically MFI P880, MFI P881, and I'd be happy to address it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as I understand it, you're done with your cross-examination with your questions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You understood correctly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think it's best to have a break now, a 20-minute break. In this way Mr. Seselj will be able to start after the break with his questions because he's going to have an hour and a half at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Seselj has the floor for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dabic, you have given two statements for The Hague Prosecutors; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And for the team assisting my Defence, you have already made eight statements; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You gave me statements that I needed for the cross-examination of some other witnesses; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your first statement consists of 39 typed pages. If I'm not mistaken, that is the lengthiest statement that appeared in these proceedings against me, and I'm impressed that you demonstrated encyclopedic knowledge about the events in eastern Herzegovina during the war. In that whole statement consisting of 39 closely typed pages, only in three places do you mention either my name or Seseljevci or volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now let us see where you do so. The first time you mention my name is in connection with the video-clips that we viewed a moment ago. These videos are -- date back to July 1991, as we were told by the Prosecution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was a time when there were no armed conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, except for some confrontation in western Herzegovina between the JNA and the Croatian rebels; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Serbs learned that the surrounding Muslims and Croats were arming and they also started to procure weapons and to hold night guard duty; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dabic, you speak the same language, but nothing can be interpreted to the benefit of the Chamber if you overlap. So please, please do not answer the questions put to you by Mr. Seselj before a little moment has elapsed. And if you are observant you will see that on your screen in front of you there's the rolling text and there is the cursor, and when the cursor stops moving that's the time when the interpretation is completed. The usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So wait for it to stop and then answer. And, Mr. Seselj, I don't need to repeat it to you but also take it easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On page 11 you mention my name for the first time and you say that these men who belonged to the group of Arsen Grahovac, Karadjordje, you called them a group; later on you called them a unit. Am I right, they were still a group here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have your statement? I would like someone to give you both your statements for the Prosecution which would facilitate things because I only have one copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you giving it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have it in Serbian. I am not familiar with B/C/S. I never learned it and I don't believe I ever will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you only need the Serbian copy, I don't need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I may. I believe Mr. Seselj is referring to the 2000 statement that was given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what we're talking about, and I'm going through that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that -- right. And that's available in e-court at -- now is MFI 880, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was one of the eight statements provided to your Defence team. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So here you refer to a group, not to a formed unit. A group of men had armed themselves and are holding night guard duty. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we saw that Arsen Grahovac was wearing civilian clothes. He's not in uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we saw that one of those armed men says that they don't trust anyone more or less and that they only recognise Martic and Seselj. Did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that is what you stated in your statement, but they said they support Karadzic, Seselj, and Martic and their efforts. So it's not as precise in the statement as it is in the clip. They never mentioned Karadzic, did they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You remember that in the summer of 1991 there were no armed conflicts between Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a minute. Let me compare page 11 with the video we saw. It's almost identical, but there's a slight problem. In the video there is no mention of Mr. Karadzic, but here we have the name of Karadzic. Why is that? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why Karadzic is being mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember well that on one occasion with a friend of mine I was going to Nevesinje and I was stopped, and this friend is from Nevesinje and he lives there. And I was stopped at a barricade and they asked for our documents, and they mentioned Karadzic as well. But Dr. Seselj and Martic were mentioned only in the video-clip. Actually, when they stopped us they asked us: Are you for Karadzic? Until they saw our documents. And when they saw our documents, they let us go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, was I popular among Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the chances were 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean chances?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were for some and not for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But at least there was one person among these night guards who considered me to be popular; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I apologise. I think I know that man. He had a nickname, Usro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why such a nickname?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. It's a funny nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Among Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had they heard that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party had been engaged in various places within the Federal Republic of Croatia in defence of Serb villages? Could you please give me yes or no answers if possible.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw that on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So did you learn on television of the great victory of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party on the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo against the Croatian police and paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard of the victory of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did the JNA defeat on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Borovo Selo. It couldn't defeat anyone in Borovo Selo. It was a Serb village in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but the village had been attacked by Croatian policemen and paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know, so I won't insist. One man mentions my name and Martic's name, that he supports us. Nice of him. How did you find such an ugly nickname? I don't know. The second time you mention my name is on page 17, that upon -- at the entry into Mostar you saw a check-point with Seselj's men armed to the teeth and wearing cockades. You heard that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party during April and May 1992 were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear who was in command of those volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I go back to this check-point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you please give me brief answers. We'll come back to the check-point. Please answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear who was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where General Perisic's headquarters were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momcilo Perisic, I think in the southern camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that next to his headquarters were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, up to 100 strong, and that they were used as an intervention unit that acted upon his orders and went where the situation was most critical?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, I hear this from you for the first time. I heard that they were in the Benkovac settlement in the garrison command, and they didn't walk around town at all, I didn't see them, because they were in an intervention unit and they were sent where they were mostly needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You heard of Klepci, Prebilovci, Tasovcici, and other Serbian villages that were surrounded. General Perisic sent them there as an intervention unit. So you hadn't heard of that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Oliver Baret --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are going much too fast and I think this is why Ms. Biersay is on her feet. Mr. Seselj, you are speaking much too fast and because of this the villages you mentioned cannot be recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Oliver Denis Baret?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I hear it from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're hearing this name from me for the first time as the commander of this unit of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, the so-called Seseljevci in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you said that Seselj's men held a check-point and I was surprised by this. What would Seselj's men be doing at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we're coming back to the check-point. When I got to Mostar, or rather, in Nevesinje and when I started off from Nevesinje - and I said this last night here in court - driving a Renault 4 vehicle, upon the entrance to the town near two petrol stations there were a group of men and I asked the policeman: Who are they? And he said that they were Seseljevci. I didn't ask where they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it customary for the military police to hold check-points?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ask yourself what would Seseljevci be doing there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were not certain that Seselj's men were holding this check-point?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it says that here. So you're not sure about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from these policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the third place you refer to Seselj's men is on page 23, and you say that in Nevesinje there were about 100 Seselj's men and about 50 armed volunteers, et cetera. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but those were probably when they were withdrawing from town, when those from the garrison command had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But what are Seselj's men doing among the people withdrawing from the garrison?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was during the withdrawal from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Seselj's men withdrew from Mostar when the JNA withdrew, and this had to be before the 25th of May, 1992, and do you know why? Because their commander, Oliver Denis Baret, was with me in Podgorica on the 25th of May. Did you hear that on the 25th of May, 1992, in Podgorica an assassination attempt was made at me, that a Muslim threw a hand-grenade at me after a rally of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear of that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you didn't hear that Oliver Denis Baret was seriously wounded, that he had several shots in his lower stomach and legs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because I've given the book to the Prosecution called the "Podgorica Assassination" with all the court documents showing that Oliver Denis Baret was one of the injured in that assassination together with Miroslav Vukovic. So they withdrew. If Oliver was in Podgorica on the 25th of May, all of them had to have withdrawn by that date. And you never heard of Branislav Vakic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I heard that name for the first time here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you heard that there were Seselj's men in Nevesinje; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard only about the garrison command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have been given a document by the Prosecution, a certificate by General Novica Grusic. Could it be placed on the ELMO, please. It is handwritten by the general on the 28th of June, 1992. Could you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe this is 65 ter number 1636, to which I referred the Court in discussing 65 ter number 1910 by Branislav Vakic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If you have not heard of Branislav Vakic, then you have never seen him in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You hadn't seen Seselj's men in Nevesinje either?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, during my stay in Mostar while I was wounded I went to Nevesinje only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So you cannot confirm that there were 100 Seselj's men in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was this put into your statement just like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that very often from people who went up there. I had no need to go to Nevesinje because my family was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's read this document. "Certificate by the commander of the war unit 7640 Nevesinje," that was later the Nevesinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th Motorised --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Confirming that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If possible, Your Honours, could we have the split screen so we could see the English. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That Branislav Vakic took part with 19 others in the liberation of Podvelezje and in crushing the enemy's front line along at Banjdol-Sipovac-Sveta Gora axis. Is that what is written here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where this Banjdol, Sipovac, and Sveta Gora are?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Vojislav Seselj, at the time of the liberation of Podvelezje, I was in the military hospital, and I know where that axis is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's the only thing I'm interested in. Keep your answers as short as possible because I don't have enough time to put all the questions that I want to put to you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know where you were and I'm not going to miss a beat.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you know where that axis or road is?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes he.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How far away is it from these localities where these mass crimes occurred later? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my estimate it must be over 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Over 35 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's pretty far away from the place where the crimes had been committed, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Throughout your statement there are only these three places where you mention me or Seselj's men, or rather, volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, which is their official name. Am I right now?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In this statement you describe in detail a large number of crimes that were committed in the territory of Nevesinje and Mostar in June 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, let us see what it is that you're describing there. First of all, when Dragan Lozo was killed, that is page 20 of your statement on the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A few soldiers took military trucks, went to Zalik and took these 78 men out of the building, Muslims they were, and about ten of them were taken to someplace where they killed them near Zalik, right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not to go into great detail. All of that is contained in my indictment and I had never heard of these places. You do not mention Seselj's men as any kind of perpetrators here. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The second place is the 14th of June in Vrapcici. 20 Muslim and Croat civilians were arrested, they were taken to the morgue at the city cemetery called Sutina, and after that they were taken to the bank of the Neretva River and they were executed there, buried, and covered by sand. That is on page 21, and there is no reference there to these people being Seselj's men or volunteers of the Serb Radical Party; right? So this --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I heard. The 13th of June when Dragan Lozo got killed, that is when I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just keep your answers as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For the Court's assistance, it's page 21 and 22 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Later on when the Muslims killed Colonel Tomislav Pusara, he was a colonel?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Podvelezje. Then a group of Serb soldiers carried out a retaliation against the Muslims in the villages of Sopi --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- I don't want to mention all the names of the villages. You did not mention at all that it was Seselj's men or the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party that took part in this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned some other names --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Everybody's speaking at the same time. Impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, please observe the instructions of the Court and speak slowly, and Mr. Witness as well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You speak about the crime at Teleca Lastva, the massacre that took place there, and you mention many names of the protagonists of that crime. Does that crime have anything to do with Seselj's men, or rather, volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, that is on page 25?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. On page 26 you talk about members of the military police who committed some crimes, organised an ambush, and then allegedly they liquidated 70 civilians. You are mentioning people here who commanded these men. Does this have anything to do with Seselj's men or volunteers of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me not go into all the names that you mention. There are some people there who are deceased and others who are alive. All right. Well, anyway, page 27. There is a reference to a crime against Muslims in the pit called Breza, which is 4 kilometres from Zijemlja. You talked about that as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that crime have anything to do with Seselj's men or volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, rather?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that crime when I got out of hospital, and no one mentioned Seselj's men, as you had put it, or the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, the seventh crime you mention, you say that that is in the territory of the 2nd Light Brigade. You also say who the commander was and who was there and whatever else, and then towards the end of June 1992 in the upper field of Nevesinje a mass crime had been committed - let me not go into all the details now. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do with the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party or Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened yet again at the time when I was in hospital. I heard that they -- that the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party or Seselj's men were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On that same page, number 27, you mention Boro Antelj, the volunteers of the SPO, Radovan Soldo, and some other people who you also identify as members of the SPO and there is no mention of Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite right. They were volunteers of the SPO and the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. The ninth crime you mention was yet again in Nevesinje itself. That must have been the expulsion of the Muslims from Nevesinje in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned the men who took part in that. Can you say that there was a single man of Seselj's there, or rather, a single volunteer of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm with certainty that not a single one was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then there is also the crime in the pit of Sehovina near Nevesinje, it is 60 metres deep. You spoke of the crime against Muslim civilians there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that crime have anything to do with Seselj's men or volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, rather?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had any one of these crimes been linked to my name or the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, would there be any reason for you not to say that to The Hague investigators in 2000? You made -- you gave this statement in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I did give that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You did not have any information that would charge me with -- or the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party with the commission of that crime?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. I was in Mostar and I said very nicely that your men, or rather, the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, Seselj's men, that I had not seen them at all in the town of Mostar. I just heard that they were up there at the garrison command, and this is the first time that I hear of Branislav Vakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because he commanded the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Please. Let us move on. Let's just not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where the Braca Fejica Street is in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a man being thrown into a pit there and that a grenade was thrown in after him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was the man?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was an ethnic Croat and a man of Albanian ethnicity threw the grenade into the pit after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So if it was a man of Albanian ethnicity then it was a conflict between Croats and Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The man who threw the grenade was a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that man have anything to do with Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could he because he was an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Judge has already reprimanded you, and he likes complaining noisily about me the most. I have adapted but you seem to be unable to adjust. So don't speak at the same time. The Prosecution has a false witness saying that this man was killed by Seselj's men. That's why I'm asking you. You're from Mostar and that's why I'm asking you about that. Have you heard of the village of Topja or Topla near Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Topla?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, if I wrote it down properly. Allegedly there is a Muslim village called Topla.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. Perhaps it was written wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how could it be written?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Topla?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tople?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about any of that and I am from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Have you heard of some Ljubo Kapor?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Kapor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's from Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was he?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the Bileca volunteers with the late Radovan Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he got killed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Kapor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have information here about a witness saying -- okay, if you don't know about it I'm not going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really know the one what was in the unit of the late Rade Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now explain the following to me.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 2004 the OTP took yet another statement from you, and now in that statement they quote some parts from the first statement and allegedly you then interject, saying, these were Seselj's men, that were Seselj's men, et cetera. Now, it says here that you said on page 2 -- I mean paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. You are now moving to the 2004 statement. I would like to stay with the 2000 statement. I've asked you this question already, but I'm trying to understand. You spent four days with the OTP back then. We have the very exact dates, on the 10th of November, the 11th of November, the 12th of November, and apparently you returned on the 13th for the statement to be read back to you. So four entire days, which explains why there are so many pages, 39 all in all. So this is a major piece of work that was done then. But when you finished the interview, did you not ask Madame St. Germain what this was going to be used for, in which proceedings? Did she say nothing to you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As much as you can remember - I know it is very difficult to remember because we're now in 2010 and that was in 2000, so that was ten years ago - didn't she tell you that this was going to be for the Seselj trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am stating to you with full argumentation that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well, the statement for me was made up only in 2004. You see how tendentious it is. They just kept putting in my name and linking it to various crimes subsequently. In 2000 they didn't even know that they would be indicting me for anything, that they would be writing up an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the second paragraph you say - and now tell me how come this is here - that Arsen Grahovac was a member of the Serb Radical Party in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, I think that that was mistranslated. I know that the late Arsen Grahovac was a member of the SPO. I'm sure that the translator/interpreter did not translate that properly for Ms. Brigitte.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in the first elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, the SPO, the Serb Renewal Movement was victorious in the local elections in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that Arsen Grahovac was a member of the Municipal Assembly of Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know about that. I hear about it from you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have here a certificate from the president of the municipality of the Nevesinje that I showed in court when another witness was being heard, to the effect that Arsen Grahovac was a member of the Municipal Assembly of Nevesinje up until the moment he was killed.
